questions.topic_title: Journey of the Holy Prophet Muhammad (pbuh)
questions.question: Describe the event of the Isra and Mi'raj, the Night Journey and Ascension. [8]
questions.model_answer:
The Isra and Mi'raj took place in about 620 CE, shortly after the Year of Sorrow in which the Prophet (PBUH) lost both Abu Talib and Khadija (RA), and it came as a consolation after the rejection at Ta'if. The Isra was the night journey: Angel Jibrail came to the Prophet (PBUH) at the Kaaba, his breast was opened and washed, and he was carried on the Buraq from the Sacred Mosque in Makkah to Masjid al-Aqsa in Jerusalem. There he led all the previous prophets in prayer, which showed that he was the final prophet and the leader of them all.

The Mi'raj was the ascension through the seven heavens. At each level he met earlier prophets, including Adam, Isa and Yahya, Yusuf, Idris, Harun, Musa and finally Ibrahim (AS) at the Bait al-Ma'mur. He was shown Sidrat al-Muntaha, the furthest lote tree, and was granted the vision of Paradise and Hellfire. In the divine presence the five daily prayers were made obligatory. Fifty prayers were prescribed at first, and on the advice of Musa (AS) the Prophet (PBUH) returned repeatedly to request a reduction until they were fixed at five, with the reward of fifty.

On returning to Makkah the same night, the Prophet (PBUH) described the journey. The Quraysh mocked him and questioned him about Jerusalem, which he described accurately although he had never seen it. Abu Bakr (RA) believed him immediately without hesitation and earned the title Al-Siddiq, the truthful one. The event is referred to in Surah Al-Isra and Surah Al-Najm. Its significance is that it confirmed the Prophet's rank, established Salah as the central act of worship and the only pillar ordained directly in the heavens, and separated sincere believers from those whose faith was weak.
questions.mark_scheme: Level 1 (1-2): Mentions a journey at night. Level 2 (3-4): Names Jerusalem or the ascension, limited detail. Level 3 (5-6): Both Isra and Mi'raj described with the Buraq, leading the prophets, and the prayers being fixed. Level 4 (7-8): Comprehensive - context after the Year of Sorrow, both stages in order, meeting named prophets, the reduction from fifty to five, and the reaction of the Quraysh and Abu Bakr (RA).

questions.topic_title: Journey of the Holy Prophet Muhammad (pbuh)
questions.question: Why did Abu Bakr (RA) earn the title Al-Siddiq after the Night Journey? [3]
questions.model_answer: When the Quraysh came to him mocking the Prophet's account of travelling to Jerusalem and back in one night, Abu Bakr (RA) did not hesitate. He replied that if the Prophet (PBUH) had said it, then it was true, and that he believed him in matters far greater than this, meaning the revelation itself. Because he accepted the report instantly and without demanding proof, he was given the title Al-Siddiq, the one who affirms the truth.

questions.topic_title: Journey of the Holy Prophet Muhammad (pbuh)
questions.question: Describe the Pledges of Aqabah and explain their importance. [6]
questions.model_answer:
The First Pledge of Aqabah took place in 621 CE, when twelve men from Yathrib met the Prophet (PBUH) secretly at Aqabah during the pilgrimage season. They pledged to worship none but Allah, not to steal, not to commit adultery, not to kill their children, not to slander, and to obey the Prophet (PBUH) in what is right. Because it contained no commitment to fight, it is known as the Pledge of Women. The Prophet (PBUH) sent Mus'ab ibn Umayr (RA) back with them to teach Islam, and through his work Islam spread quickly in Yathrib.

The Second Pledge took place the following year, 622 CE, when seventy-three men and two women came. They pledged not only to accept Islam but to protect the Prophet (PBUH) as they would protect their own families, which meant a commitment to fight if necessary. They chose twelve representatives to lead their people.

Their importance is that they gave the Muslims a secure base outside Makkah for the first time, and made the Hijrah possible: the Prophet (PBUH) now had a city that had invited him and undertaken to defend him. They transformed Islam from a persecuted movement into a community with territory, and led directly to the founding of the first Islamic state in Madinah.
questions.mark_scheme: Level 1 (1-2): Mentions a pledge made at Aqabah. Level 2 (3-4): Describes one pledge with some terms. Level 3 (5-6): Both pledges described with dates and numbers, the difference between them explained, and the link to the Hijrah made clear.

questions.topic_title: Journey of the Holy Prophet Muhammad (pbuh)
questions.question: Why did the Prophet (PBUH) travel to Ta'if, and what happened there? [4]
questions.model_answer: In 619 CE, after the deaths of Abu Talib and Khadija (RA) left him without protection in Makkah, the Prophet (PBUH) travelled to Ta'if with Zayd ibn Haritha (RA) to invite the tribe of Thaqif to Islam and to seek their support. Their leaders rejected him rudely and set the street children on him, who pelted him with stones until his feet bled. He took shelter in an orchard, where he made the well-known supplication complaining of his weakness to Allah rather than against the people. Angel Jibrail came with the angel of the mountains, offering to crush the town between two mountains, but the Prophet (PBUH) refused and said he hoped their descendants would worship Allah alone. In the orchard the slave Addas accepted Islam. The journey shows both the depth of the opposition he faced and his mercy towards those who rejected him.

questions.question: Explain the Muslim belief in angels. [6]
questions.model_answer: Belief in angels is the second article of faith. Muslims believe angels are beings created by Allah from light, who have no free will to disobey Him and who carry out His commands exactly. They do not eat, drink, sleep, marry or have gender, and they can take human form when required, as Jibrail did when appearing as Dihyah al-Kalbi. Their number is known only to Allah, but several are named with specific duties: Jibrail (AS) brought revelation to the prophets; Mika'il (AS) is responsible for rain and sustenance; Israfil (AS) will blow the trumpet on the Day of Judgement; and Izra'il, the angel of death, takes souls. Munkar and Nakir question the dead in the grave. The Kiraman Katibin record every person's deeds, and other angels guard human beings by Allah's command. The importance of this belief is that it reminds a Muslim that his actions are always witnessed and recorded, which encourages honesty even in private. It also confirms the reliability of revelation, since the Quran was brought by Jibrail (AS), an angel incapable of altering the message.
questions.mark_scheme: Level 1 (1-2): States that angels exist and are made of light. Level 2 (3-4): Describes their nature and names one or two with duties. Level 3 (5-6): Full account of their nature, several named angels with their specific duties, and the effect of the belief on a Muslim's conduct.

questions.question: Explain the Muslim belief in predestination (Taqdir) and how it affects a believer's life. [6]
questions.model_answer:
Taqdir is the sixth article of faith and means that Allah has knowledge of all things and that nothing occurs except by His will and decree. He knows what has happened, what is happening and what will happen, and this knowledge was recorded before creation. Muslims believe this does not remove human responsibility, because Allah has also given human beings the power to choose between right and wrong; His knowing what a person will choose does not force that choice. This is why people are still accountable on the Day of Judgement.

The effect on a believer's life is considerable. It brings patience and contentment in hardship, because loss, illness and difficulty are understood as part of a plan rather than as meaningless accident. It removes arrogance in success, since ability and opportunity come from Allah. It removes despair and the fear of other people, because no harm can reach a person except by Allah's permission. At the same time it does not permit passivity: the Prophet (PBUH) told the man who left his camel untied to tie it and then trust in Allah, which shows that a Muslim must take proper means and then accept the outcome.
questions.mark_scheme: Level 1 (1-2): States that everything is decided by Allah. Level 2 (3-4): Explains the belief with some reference to human responsibility. Level 3 (5-6): Explains the belief fully, resolves the tension with free will and accountability, and gives practical effects supported by an example such as tying the camel.

questions.question: Describe the contribution of Hazrat Abu Bakr (RA) to Islam during the lifetime of the Prophet (PBUH). [6]
questions.model_answer: Abu Bakr (RA) was the first free adult man to accept Islam, and his acceptance carried great weight because he was respected as an honest merchant, which brought others such as Uthman, Talha and Zubair (RA) to Islam through him. He spent his wealth freely, buying and freeing tortured slaves including Bilal (RA). He affirmed the Night Journey without hesitation and earned the title Al-Siddiq. He was the Prophet's only companion on the Hijrah, hiding with him in the Cave of Thawr, where the Quran records the Prophet (PBUH) comforting him with the words do not grieve, for Allah is with us. He gave his daughter Aisha (RA) in marriage to the Prophet (PBUH). He fought in all the major battles, and at Tabuk he gave the whole of his wealth to equip the Army of Hardship, saying he had left Allah and His Messenger for his family. In the Prophet's final illness he was appointed to lead the congregational prayers, which the community later understood as an indication of his fitness to lead.
questions.mark_scheme: Level 1 (1-2): States that he was the first caliph or a close companion. Level 2 (3-4): Two or three contributions named with limited detail. Level 3 (5-6): A full range covering his early acceptance, freeing of slaves, the Hijrah, his giving at Tabuk, and leading the prayer in the Prophet's illness.

questions.question: Describe the contribution of Hazrat Khadija (RA) to the early Muslim community. [4]
questions.model_answer: Khadija (RA) was the first person of all to accept Islam, believing the Prophet (PBUH) immediately when he returned frightened from the Cave of Hira. She comforted him, reminding him of his good character and his care for the poor, and took him to her cousin Waraqah ibn Nawfal, who confirmed that what had come to him was the same angel who had come to Musa (AS). She supported the mission with her entire wealth, which sustained the Muslims through the years of persecution and the boycott of Banu Hashim. She stood by the Prophet (PBUH) through every hardship and never wavered, and he never married another woman during her lifetime. Her death in 619 CE was so great a loss that the year is called the Year of Sorrow.
